cases.name: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive / clubhouse)
cases.address: 3 North Castle Drive, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Eagle Ridge

timeline.summary: The board granted an extension of time for Eagle Ridge on a quick motion with no substantive discussion.
Procedural item: the board granted an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge application with no discussion.
The board granted an extension of time for Eagle Ridge, which is working through a brownfield designation for orchard-related soil before potentially advancing a different development.
The board approved an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge final subdivision.

The board granted an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge subdivision, which is awaiting Department of Health sign-off (verbal approval received) before final condition checks with the town's consultants.

The board discussed the pesticide/herbicide soil contamination on the site being handled through the DEC Brownfield/BCP program, the roughly 30,000 cubic yards of soil to be trucked out, phasing, and buyer disclosure, then granted a 90-day extension of time.

Request for an extension of time on the Eagle Ridge subdivision. The applicant reported the Mylar had been submitted to the County Health Department but review had stalled because the reviewing staffer was out for about a month with no clear hand-off. The board granted the extension of time.

The applicant's attorney requested an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge subdivision and site plan. The subdivision plat is still with the county Department of Health for execution, but all other outstanding items (easements, etc.) have been completed, with the DOH being the only hold-up; completion is hoped for by spring 2026. The board had no questions and approved both the subdivision extension and the site plan extension.

As a condition of the 2024 master site plan approval, the applicant returned for site plan approval of a two-story, ~5,100 sq ft clubhouse with pool, bocce, pickleball, and an event lawn. Parking was short - 56 spaces required versus 26 provided at the building plus dispersed visitor spaces - and the board declined to let visitor parking be double-counted, voting to refer the applicant to the ZBA for a parking variance. The dominant concern was tall tiered retaining walls (12 to 13.5 feet) facing the community park, which the board found too industrial; the applicant offered landscaping screening, stamped/colored concrete, and staking. The board scheduled a site visit for the following Wednesday and acknowledged receipt of the town engineer's bond memo.

The board handled a routine request for an extension of time for Eagle Ridge. A member reported an update from Corey indicating the applicant is able to move forward and obtain the final sign-off, so this should be the last extension needed. The chair made a motion to grant the extension and it passed. Brief confirmation was given that the DEP paperwork was in order.

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road
cases.address: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Jerry Tortarella (Hocherman Tortorella & Wexler), attorney; Tim Allen (Bibbo Associates)

trajectory.status: public hearing continued/adjourned to first September meeting
public hearing continued | adjourned to Nov 10

timeline.summary: Introductory review of two related wetland applications: shifting/reworking golf putting greens and access paths on 92 (originally permitted administratively in 1999) and remediation of path work behind a pool on 94 that had drawn a building-department violation resolved by plea; treated as a Type II action, the board directed a site walk and referral to the Conservation Board, with a functional wetland analysis to follow.

Discussion of after-the-fact wetlands/buffer disturbance (a reconstructed golf hole on 92 and unpermitted pool work on 94) with a conservation-board-endorsed 2-to-1 mitigation and 5-year monitoring plan; the board wanted the debris/shed and stored fuels cleaned up and a site walk done before voting, and scheduled a public hearing for the second February meeting.

Combined public hearing on site plan, wetlands, and tree-removal permits for a golf green/tees on 92 and a pool renovation and access path on 94, following a building-department violation for pool work and path creation without permits; multiple neighbors and two attorneys objected on safety, wetlands, tree-clearing, and commercial-use grounds, and after an executive session the board kept the hearing open and asked staff to research the approval history while the applicant addresses neighbor concerns.

The reopened public hearing proceeded even though the applicant's representative failed to appear and the application had not changed since the last meeting; neighbors reiterated safety and wetland concerns and the board discussed how to constrain the greens and tees before adjourning the hearing.

timeline.status: public hearing continued/adjourned to first September meeting
timeline.summary: Continuation of the hearing on after-the-fact wetlands and site-plan approval for golf features on two adjoining wetland-buffer properties: one retained (unfinished) green, two sand traps, a constructed tee box (T1) and three additional turf tee positions (T2-T4), plus paths and a shed. The applicant argued the tees are de minimis, non-structural, that no golf-ball incidents have occurred in 26 years, and that setbacks for pools/tennis courts do not apply. Neighbor Barry Edelman (88 Round Hill Road) opposed through counsel, stressing safety of children/grandchildren, the green sitting only 8-16 feet from the shared line, trajectories aimed at his glass-walled house, intensification from two to four tees, and requesting a 30-foot setback, DEC review, and stronger screening. After an executive session with counsel, the board indicated it favors retaining the green with a robust landscape and net mitigation plan along the 88 line but wants T3 and T4 eliminated, and directed the applicant to pursue DEC and a building-inspector determination. Adjourned to the first September meeting.

Reopened (re-noticed) public hearing on renovation/expansion of existing golf greens and tees, plus wetlands and tree-removal permits. The applicant removed two proposed tees, submitted a buffer/screening landscape plan (12 trees, 54 shrubs), and brought a golf pro to argue the short hole poses little errant-ball risk. Neighbors (Kalindi Bhat at 98, and Barry Edelman at 88 via counsel) pressed safety concerns about golf balls crossing property lines. The Board debated whether the 1998 legalization (via the Conservation Board's wetlands permit) binds this review, and discussed adding a low deflector screen/netting near the tees. No vote due to the short board; hearing left open and adjourned to Oct 27, with the applicant to show the screening on the plan.

timeline.status: public hearing continued | adjourned to Nov 10
timeline.summary: Continued wetlands-permit hearing for an existing golf putting green and two tee boxes. The applicant proposed a localized 10-ft-wide by 6-ft-high net above the upper tee plus deflectors to protect the neighbor. Chairman Carthy floated conceptual town legislation to regulate putting greens (treat greens as structures respecting side-yard setbacks, and limit tee distance to 3x the setback), while stressing it would not govern this application. The board pressed the applicant to pull the tees closer to the green so only chip/pitch shots are used, add netting at the road-side tee, and add evergreen screening near the OWTS; the applicant argued a 25-year no-incident history. The hearing was adjourned to Nov 10 for a revised plan and a resolution vote.

The chair announced at the outset that the public hearing for 92 & 94 Round Hill Road had been moved off the agenda for the evening and would be covered on another night. No substantive discussion occurred. The board confirmed whether anyone in the audience was present for the item before moving on.

The applicant's attorney appeared without the applicant, who was unavailable, and asked to carry the continued hearing to the second January meeting to allow time to review draft approval documents with the client over the holidays. He reported the client elected to remove retaining-wall segment 'T1' entirely and submitted revised plans reflecting that. The neighbor's counsel spoke constructively, praising progress and raising administrative cleanups (drawing revision dates, papering the T1 removal, an as-built condition, a null-and-void-on-alteration clause, and whether the T2 netting should also be netted on top). The board reopened, took the neighbor's comments, and re-adjourned to January 26, 2026.

cases.name: 40 High Street
cases.applicant: Corey Salman (Zarin & Steinmetz), attorney; Peter Gregory, engineer

timeline.summary: Public hearing on a two-lot subdivision of a ~5.8-acre R-1A parcel (lots of 1.25 and 4.59 acres); after confirming the frontage area is a drainage ditch rather than regulated wetland and reviewing stormwater and septic, the board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the preliminary and final subdivision plats as amended, with a note added that future homes return to the Planning Board.
The board granted an extension of time for 40 High Street; a member asked why the extension was requested but no specific reason was provided beyond an attached letter.
The board granted an extension of time because the approval could not be signed before it was set to expire.
The board granted an extension of time for this application, which is awaiting review at the county Health Department.
The board granted a routine extension of time; the applicant is still working through the Department of Health.

Extension of time request. Corey explained they were close to finishing the milk hour/health department submission when their DOH reviewer left and a new reviewer issued additional comments on August 1, which they are now addressing. The board granted the extension of time.
The board granted a requested extension of time, attributed to ongoing health department (septic) issues. Handled quickly by motion and unanimous voice vote.

The board considered another extension of time for 40 High Street, which has been pending since 2024. Staff reported the applicant had previously been waiting on the health department. The chair expressed impatience that it has dragged on and asked staff to find out the status before the next return. The board granted the extension.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road (National Fire Sprinklers)
cases.address: 76 Virginia Road, North White Plains, NY
cases.applicant: John Luciano / National Lawn Sprinklers (reps. Tony Vinesiana, Ron, engineer Franz Lackey/SESI)

timeline.summary: First review of a ~24,000 sf flex warehouse requiring roughly 70 feet of rock cut, a retaining-wall system up to ~50-71 ft, ~40,000 yards of material and ~2,000 truck trips, plus a green/blue roof and stormwater vaults; the board discussed the applicant's as-of-right, lot-coverage relief (47% vs 40%), blasting vs chipping, and truck traffic, then declared itself lead agency and directed referrals to the county and emergency services.

Discussion of a new warehouse/office complex on a vacant rock-outcrop lot requiring a large rock cut (~30,000+ cubic yards), anchored/gunite-stabilized walls up to 60 feet, and stormwater detention. The board raised concerns about FAR (interior warehouse parking counting as floor area), the scale and duration of excavation, blasting vs chipping, and mid-job stoppage risk; it referred the FAR variance to the Zoning Board of Appeals and asked for a full construction/excavation/geotechnical package.

Non-hearing discussion of a warehouse-and-office proposal requiring a large rock cut and slope stabilization; the applicant's geotechnical engineer walked through the soil-nail and controlled rock-removal method, and the board decided the town must hire its own geotechnical engineer, with an FAR variance still pending at the ZBA and a public hearing still to come.

Discussion of a substantial rock-excavation and retaining-wall project. Following a prior board directive, a town geotechnical engineer (Carlin Simpson) reviewed the applicant's plans and, after 21 test pits and eight borings with geophysical scanning, reported that roughly 99% of requested data had been provided, with only anchor pull-out loads still to be translated onto the plans. The engineer described a controlled, no-blasting method (line drilling, chopping/feather splitting in 10-foot lifts, draped ring-net systems with rock anchors, vibration monitoring, existing-condition surveys within 500 feet) over a three-to-four-month timeframe. The board pressed on safety and what happens if something is 'missed,' and agreed to schedule a public hearing (targeted for December 8) with the geotechnical engineer present. Counsel raised SEQRA: the action is unlisted, a full EAF was requested, and the ZBA variance may need to be revisited because SEQRA was not completed before it.

The applicant presented a reduced 15,000 sq ft flex warehouse/office (FAR variance already granted) requiring a large six-on-one rock cut with soil nails, rock anchors, and steel mesh netting on a steep slope 12-15 feet from Miller Hill Park, a Revolutionary War battlefield. The applicant's geotechnical team and the town-retained peer reviewer, Bob Simpson (Carlin Simpson Associates), testified the design is achievable with only minor open technical items and confirmed no blasting is proposed. Extensive public comment opposed or questioned the project on catastrophic-slope-failure risk, historic preservation, water/sewer capacity, dust, truck logistics, and long-term (50+ year) maintenance liability, and Open Space chair Carrie Kayza detailed alleged misrepresentations in the applicant's environmental assessment form (SHPO consultation, air pollutants, critical environmental area). The board secured the applicant's consent to a no-blasting condition on the site plan and adjourned the hearing to gather more on the EAF, construction oversight, and a maintenance covenant/deed restriction.

Reopened hearing on a project involving a substantial rock cut stabilized by an anchored netting system, tied to bringing the applicant's nearby office property into conformance. The applicant reported a completed Phase 1A archaeological study (no/low sensitivity, submitted to and accepted by SHPO) and the board adopted an amended negative declaration removing a mischaracterized historical-society letter reference. Major unresolved items kept the hearing open: a written seismic/vibration monitoring plan for the town engineer to review, a deeded perpetual maintenance obligation plus bonding, whether a maintenance bond also covers repair/re-pinning after a rock dislodgement, and a truck-staging/queuing plan for a project projecting ~20 trucks a day for months. Public speakers raised the NEG DEC wording and challenged anchor lengths, safety, and whether an alternate design was considered.

After roughly six weeks of work, the board closed the public hearing and adopted a conditioned site-plan resolution for a landscaping-business building requiring a large rock cut (up to ~70 feet, chipping not blasting, no on-site crushing) with a soil-nailed/netted retaining wall. Extensive discussion covered a seismic/vibration/air/noise monitoring plan with stop-work exceedance thresholds and town notifications, a truck-routing safety plan queuing trucks off-site, an annual operating permit and wall-maintenance manual traveling with the deed, and a Phase 1B archaeological survey (nothing on site; high Revolutionary-War sensitivity next door at Miller Hill). A long exchange on insurance and catastrophic-failure risk resolved into a condition requiring the owner to maintain reasonable liability/property insurance to the satisfaction of the town attorney.

cases.name: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road
cases.address: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road, North Castle, NY

timeline.summary: The board granted an extension of time for the approved application at 124 Old Mount Kisco Road (paid extension).
The board granted an extension of time (noted as roughly the 12th) after the applicant explained focus had shifted to other projects that are now wrapping up so work can proceed on 124 and 130.
The board granted an extension of time for this application after the applicant's engineer submitted materials the same day.

cases.name: 154 Lafayette Avenue (Mistis Transport)
cases.applicant: Michael Miele
cases.lastStatus: public hearing opened and closed; approved with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing opened and closed; approved with conditions

timeline.summary: First introduction of a proposal to legalize unpermitted work by converting a nonconforming single-family house in the industrial (INDA) district to office/storage use; the board asked the applicant to clean up the plan, consider consolidating the three lots he controls, address off-street parking (possibly via ZBA), and deal with the outstanding violations.

Discussion of converting a house to office use; the board pressed the applicant to address parking deficiencies comprehensively across three commonly owned Lafayette Avenue parcels rather than piecemeal, and to resolve multiple building-department notices of violation, directing a meeting with the chair and building inspector.

The board reviewed a revised plan to remove a lot line and combine two of three properties, keep an existing non-conforming residence, convert a building to an office, store 16 commercial vehicles, and add parking, then referred the applicant to the ZBA and Town Board for the necessary variances and license.

Discussion of a site plan for a business relying on outdoor truck storage (19 truck spaces in back). The Police Department objected to proposed front parking spaces that would sit partly in the right-of-way and require vehicles to back into the road, calling it a new hazardous condition rather than a memorialized existing one. The board explored alternatives at length: parallel parking in front, angle parking, stacking trucks, and having drivers park cars in the truck spaces they vacate, plus relocating ADA spaces nearer the accessible ramp. No decision was made; the applicant was asked to prepare a parallel-parking layout and a narrative (with distances to the pavement) to bring back, potentially for the Police, Zoning Board of Appeals, and Town Board.

Discussion of a plan to establish an office, merge lots/move a lot line, and store US-mail delivery trucks. The applicant originally proposed perpendicular parking partly in the right-of-way, but the police department recommended against it and the town code prohibits it; the applicant returned with six parallel spaces. The board debated at length whether parallel (respecting the police) or perpendicular (which neighbors do under grandfathered variances) better serves the site, given early-morning (3-5am) truck turnover and a possible 'demolition derby' of drivers arriving at once. The owner spoke passionately, feeling singled out relative to neighbors who park outside. The board ultimately directed the applicant to move forward with the parallel-parking plan as presented and scheduled a public hearing, reasoning that pursuing perpendicular would require ZBA/town-board approvals and delay.

timeline.status: public hearing opened and closed; approved with conditions
timeline.summary: Change of use of a legal non-conforming home to office use, treating three existing non-conforming parcels together by moving a property line, removing one dwelling and converting another to an office, plus commercial truck storage. The long-standing sticking point was parking; the board reaffirmed acceptance of six parallel spaces in front and required the plan to clearly show the nine off-street spaces needed for the office kept truck-free, with the balance available for overnight truck storage. It was determined ARB review was unnecessary (no exterior changes) and that whether ZBA approval is needed turns on a building-inspector determination of whether the nonconformity is increased. The board struck a condition, adopted the NegDec, the site-plan resolution, and the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.

cases.name: 113 King Street (RCLA Enclave at Armonk / Toll)
cases.applicant: Airport Campus (applicant represented by counsel; planner Adam preparing resolutions)

timeline.summary: Wrap-up discussion of a multifamily townhouse project with a clubhouse; the board reviewed draft findings statement and site plan/subdivision resolutions, resolved engineering/water-sewer conditions, discussed adding first-floor-bedroom and 45 dBA noise conditions, and flagged a school-bus routing/sight-line concern on Cooney Hill Road, aiming for final action on the 11th pending ARB approval.

The board adopted the SEQRA findings statement (consistent with the town board's) and approved the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions as amended, dated March 11, 2024; site plan approval was withheld because the applicant has not yet obtained ARB approval. Members debated the roughly 70 conditions but staff confirmed most were routine engineering items.
The board granted a routine extension of time; the applicant reported substantial progress on conditions but still needs DEP/SWPPP approval and county health department sign-off.

The applicant appealed an RPRC decision that referred it back to the ARB to finalize color-scheme distribution and per-lot landscaping across the 125-unit development. The applicant argued the ARB approval already provided for randomly distributed one-third/one-third/one-third color schemes and that reappearing was unnecessary and conflicting. After discussion, the Board granted the appeal but secured a commitment that the applicant will provide a progress report to the planner (Adam) at the one-third construction mark to give the ARB oversight of the distribution. Motion to grant the appeal passed.

A field-change request after a CAD software error caused the water-tank foundation, pumping station, and generator to be built roughly 10 feet north of the approved location, with minor adjustments to spacing between the components; the generator remains six feet from the property line and everything stays zoning-compliant. With no board questions, the resolution was adopted.

cases.name: 12 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: John Jay Scarla Jr. (architect)

timeline.summary: Review of a plan to renovate a historic structure into a law office in the front and residential duplex in the rear, remove the barn/shed, and build a rear parking lot; the board worked through driveway width, buffer/screening and clearance so delivery vehicles won't hit the building, and directed the applicant to LPC (certificate of appropriateness), ARB, and possibly the ZBA before scheduling a public hearing.

With the applicant absent, the board referred the application to the ZBA for an off-street parking variance (seven spaces shown, nine required) and a variance for the sub-20-foot driveway width along the house.

Public hearing opened for converting a historic house into a front office plus rear apartment; a neighbor voiced extensive opposition and the applicant's plans lacked current engineering, an updated eight-space parking layout, and landscape/lighting details, so the board kept the hearing open pending revised submissions.

The board reopened and closed the hearing on converting the house to an office with one residential unit, reviewing the landscape/screening plan, parking (eight spaces incl. one handicap), lighting, stormwater, and ARB/historic-preservation approvals, then adopted the site-plan approval.

A brief extension-of-time request for a project involving a driveway to reach the rear of the property, described as very close to final approval with the applicant anxious to proceed. The board granted the extension, then closed the Planning Board for 2025.

cases.name: 9 Barnard Road
cases.applicant: Mr. Gentile

timeline.summary: Discussion item where the board acts in an advisory capacity to the building department over fill imported without a permit. The applicant's attorney and consultant argued prior testing (with slightly elevated but acceptable lead) was sufficient, while the town's HES consultant recommended a more rigorous DEC Part 360 sampling protocol. The board directed the applicant to comply with the HES testing protocol before the fill could be allowed to remain.

Continued discussion of a stone retaining wall built without a permit (~150 ft long, a section over 6 ft, up to ~9 ft near the street). The board reiterated its 18-month-old April 2023 direction to step the existing wall back and cap it at four feet with a tiered second wall and plantings, while the applicant pushed a grade-and-bury alternative and ultimately declined to prepare new plans, asking the board to deny the six submitted plans. The board declined to issue denials (which would force fill removal) and left it at an impasse, with soil-contamination testing still outstanding.
Item was removed from tonight's agenda; the board hopes to take it up at a future meeting.

Public hearing on legalizing an existing ~7-year-old unpermitted wall, fill, grading, tree removal and shed; the applicant proposed adding ~8 cubic yards of fill and four trees to lower the wall exposure below six feet rather than tiering it. The board rejected this, found itself at an impasse because the applicant refused to tier/reduce the wall as previously directed, closed the public hearing, and directed staff to prepare a resolution of denial for the next meeting.
With the public hearing previously closed, the board adopted the draft resolution after amending the language of a passage quoting a board member.

cases.name: 12 Seymour Place East
cases.applicant: Property owner (not present)
cases.lastStatus: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

timeline.summary: The board reviewed a detached garage over 800 sq ft (requiring a special use permit), a new pool and cabana, retaining walls and a formal lawn; no objection in principle, but floor plans and elevations are needed and the engineer must confirm stormwater/drainage given prior water issues at the site.

Discussion of a pool, cabana and detached three-car garage (garage exceeds 800 sq ft accessory-structure threshold; land coverage roughly 900 sq ft over the allowable). The board scheduled a site walk and voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the gross land-coverage variance so the ZBA and site work could proceed concurrently, with ARB and a public hearing to follow.

Post-site-walk discussion of a garage addition and rear pool complex; the board had no substantive objections and directed the applicant to obtain a GLA (floor-area) variance from the ZBA before scheduling the public hearing at a July meeting.

Opened public hearing for new pool, spa, patios, an open covered cabana, and a detached carport over 800 sq ft (special use permit); a variance for gross land coverage and accessory-structure FAR was already granted by the ZBA. Discussion centered almost entirely on drainage: the neighborhood has significant runoff draining to the cul-de-sac, and the town engineer wanted the applicant to verify the existing infiltration system/swale is working and to consider diverting proposed stormwater to the rear toward Tripling Lane rather than adding cul-tec units to a failing system. Neighbor Brian Kaminer testified to worsening street flooding. The Board scheduled a site walk (next Wednesday) and kept the hearing open.

timeline.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions
timeline.summary: Reopened hearing focused on cul-de-sac drainage. Following a site walk with town engineer John Kellard, the applicant split the drainage systems so the new garage has its own dedicated infiltration system (both designed to hold up to a 100-year storm with zero discharge), added a trench drain at the driveway bottom tied to the town culvert, converted lawn to planted meadow, and will confirm/repair the existing overflow pipe to the town system. The board closed the hearing and adopted the (date-amended) resolution, with the standing stormwater-mitigation condition delegated to the town engineer administratively.

cases.name: 100 Buckout Road
cases.applicant: Malik Samad, owner/applicant; Nicholas Shariah, Hudson Engineering; John Scarlato, architect

timeline.summary: Discussion of a proposed 3,700 sq ft new house replacing an existing dwelling on a lot with a cottage that will remain, referred by the RPRC to both the Planning Board and Conservation Board for steep-slope, wetland-buffer and grading impacts. The engineer corrected the plan to show two trees removed (not seven), described disturbing roughly 10,830 sq ft of steep slopes (largely bare rock outcroppings) and noted nearly all work sits within the wetland buffer, with the septic location constrained by the health department. To reduce impact, the applicant offered to eliminate a walk-out basement door and cut rock removal from about 12 feet to 4-5 feet near the wetlands. The board scheduled a joint site walk for November 19 at 8:30am and referred the application to the Conservation Board for concurrent review.

The board discussed 100 Buckout Road following a site walk, where the town engineer (John Kellard) suggested revisions to handle grading changes and the applicant's engineer Nick prepared a revised plan the board had not yet seen. The main procedural question was whether the wetland permit could be handled administratively as a minor permit rather than requiring Conservation Board review; the Conservation Board chair (George) confirmed by text that the sidewalk work is very minor with no need for board review. The board debated timing for a December versus January public hearing and agreed to move toward a public hearing, with a draft resolution finding the wetland permit minor and processing it administratively with town engineer input.

The applicant sought site plan, wetlands permit, and tree removal approvals for a new house. Because the engineer's review memo was far from resolved, the chair opened and adjourned the hearing. The applicant's engineer flagged disagreements on whether an NOI is required (under an acre of disturbance, not in the East-of-Hudson watershed), driveway drainage constraints between existing and proposed septic systems, staying under the one-acre wetland-buffer disturbance threshold, and rock removal on the south side for the sunroom/walkout. Missing ARB approval was also noted. The board directed the applicant to tighten the plans and reconcile the memo before returning.

Reopened continued public hearing on a new residence involving steep-slope and wetland-buffer disturbance. The applicant argued that many draft resolution conditions (retaining wall, tree count, earthwork, soil testing/infiltration, silt fence) were repeat comments already addressed, and asked to be voted on tonight. The board would not approve: an SHPO/historic-cemetery notification and a tax-map-versus-survey boundary discrepancy remained open, and, most significantly, roughly an acre of wetland mitigation for about a half acre of buffer disturbance had been steered toward administrative handling by the town wetland consultant rather than the Conservation Board. The board concluded that no site directive could authorize skipping the Conservation Board, directed the applicant to prepare a full mitigation plan and route it through the Conservation Board, and to re-notice the public hearing, targeting the May meeting.

This was a continuation of a public hearing on a wetlands permit that the board had previously declined to treat as a minor permit, sending the applicant back to the Conservation Board. The Conservation Board reviewed the home mitigation plan, found the structure could not be moved out of the buffer, judged the mitigation (slightly more than 2:1) adequate, and recommended approval. The applicant also confirmed via SHIPO that the project would not impact the African American historic cemetery across the street, and a previously missing page of engineering conditions was now reflected in the draft resolution. The board closed the public hearing and approved the resolution.

cases.name: 448 Bedford Road (church nursery-school)
cases.applicant: Steve Veneruso (Veneruso, Curto, Schwartz & Curto), attorney; Tom Curto/Carroll, architect

timeline.summary: Introductory review of a request to amend a 1983 special use permit (which allowed two classrooms) to legalize the six classrooms the ~30-year-old nursery school actually operates, with added egress; the board explained the parallel special-permit track through the Town Board and directed the applicant to compile the outstanding items from staff comments before referral.

The board reviewed a special use permit amendment to legalize the nursery school's long-standing expansion from two to six classrooms; it recommended the town board issue the permit and referred the applicant to the zoning board for an outdoor-recreation-space variance.

Having secured its amended special use permit and a ZBA variance to expand from two to six classrooms, the applicant sought site plan approval; two open items remained (delineating/striping the required parking spaces and demonstrating adequate parking-lot lighting), which the board asked to be resolved before a public hearing is scheduled.
Routine extension of time for a church's previously approved additional classrooms for its nursery school. Granted without discussion.

cases.name: 16 Davis Drive - three-car garage, driveway and fill (Paul Goudis)
cases.applicant: Paul Goudis (rep. Rick Bollinger, engineer)

timeline.summary: Early review of driveway repaving/widening, a three-car garage extension, driveway piers, a six-foot deer fence and screening, requiring a large coverage variance; the board raised the unpermitted fill already placed, driveway access depth, reducing impervious area, and possible wetland/hydric-soil impacts, and scheduled a site walk.

Imported fill tested clean; the application involves a covered parking area, driveway work near a federally-regulated (Army Corps class II) wetland buffer, land-coverage exceedance, and ~11,000 sq ft of steep-slope disturbance. The board referred it to the ZBA for coverage and noted conservation board (wetlands permit) and ARB steps remain.

The board reviewed an update on a garage/patio addition and driveway work; the applicant is pursuing a gross land coverage variance at the ZBA and has resolved conservation and stormwater concerns, with the board agreeing to send a favorable communication to the ZBA and schedule a public hearing pending soil test results and the conservation memo.

Public hearing on a site plan with tree-removal, steep-slope and wetlands permits for an attached three-car garage, driveway improvements and fill/regrading with a new stormwater/infiltration system; approved as amended with a condition to add seven arborvitae for neighbor screening.

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue (restaurant)
cases.applicant: Remix (Tony Vinesiano, attorney; Stefan, owner)

trajectory.status: extension of time granted, then flagged; variance validity referred to town attorney and ZBA

timeline.summary: Continued public hearing on a restaurant with an off-street parking variance relying on valet and shared/leased parking at 12 and 20 Maple plus the American Legion; the board closed the hearing and approved the site plan 4-1, adding conditions requiring a town-board community benefits agreement and incorporating the H&H traffic-consultant letter.

The board granted an extension of time together with a field-change notification for a facade modification (fewer windows, metal roof extended to the building edge, and photochromatic skylights) that had already been reviewed by the ARB.

timeline.status: extension of time granted, then flagged; variance validity referred to town attorney and ZBA
timeline.summary: The applicant sought an extension of time on a previously approved restaurant site plan, reporting secured funding, an ARB-approved revised exterior, and a request tied to the new town employee parking lot. The board granted the extension, but Michael Pollack then raised Town Code Section 355-77, arguing that the ZBA parking variance (issued Dec 7, 2023) had expired after two years because no building permit or CO had been issued, and that without a valid variance there is no site plan to extend. Town attorney 'Mary' agreed there is a two-year limit and would investigate, and planner Adam Kaufman noted variances can be extended by the ZBA. The board concluded the applicant likely must return to the ZBA for a variance extension and then get re-approved by the Planning Board.

At the prior meeting the board had approved an extension of time for 12 April Avenue, but it emerged that the applicant's ZBA variance had already expired and no extension was sought before it lapsed, rendering the variance and therefore the site plan null and void. The board voted to rescind its prior approval of the extension of time.

cases.name: Seminary / St. Nurses addition, 46 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: Saint Nersess Armenian Seminary (Robert Sarafian, architect)

timeline.summary: The board reviewed a proposed two-story addition for guest lecturers and a small detached residence for the retiring dean, then referred the applicant to the ZBA for an area variance from the doubled front/side-yard setback required for churches in a residential district; stormwater on Seymour to be walked with the town engineer.

The applicant combined a previously two-building proposal into a single addition to the married-students building to solve sanitary-line elevation problems, having secured a side-yard variance and ARB approval; the board reviewed grading, septic/well capacity, runoff and a proposed rain garden and agreed to schedule a public hearing (targeting the second September meeting) once the SWPPP is submitted.
The board opened the public hearing, found no neighbors present, and adjourned the hearing to the next meeting.

Continuation of the public hearing for a two-story addition creating married-student quarters and a retired-dean residence at the rear of a former barn; with no public present the board closed the hearing and adopted a resolution approving the site plan.

cases.name: 1613 Old Orchard Street
cases.address: 1613 Old Orchard Street, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Marlene Doran
cases.lastStatus: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

timeline.summary: Discussion of a new house on a vacant Quarry Heights lot where the driveway cannot meet the 200-foot sight distance requirement, requiring a ZBA variance. The board questioned the claimed clear sight line to the east and asked the applicant to return with a sight-distance profile and dimensions before being referred to the ZBA.

The board reviewed a reduced-footprint single-family house within a wetland buffer and referred the driveway sight-distance variance (164 feet looking left vs. 200 required) to the ZBA, declining to attach a positive recommendation per its practice for individual residences.

Counsel gave a full status recap of this long-running application (since January 2023) for a single-family residence on a vacant lot largely within the regulated wetland buffer. The footprint was reduced ~500 sq ft per Conservation Board conditions, and superimposed aerial coverage analysis showed building and impervious coverage fall within the range of surrounding lots. A driveway location with adequate site distances was designed with traffic engineers and a ZBA variance was granted in June. Engineer John Kellard raised remaining comments on basement elevation/drainage and unclear tree-removal designation; the board directed the applicant toward noticing a public hearing at the next meeting.

timeline.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions
timeline.summary: The applicant proposed a new two-story, four-bedroom colonial (~3,000 sq ft living area, ~4,000 sq ft gross) on a vacant lot, with nearly all disturbance in the wetland buffer, municipal sewer connection, and a mitigation plan the Conservation Board had recommended (conditioned on footprint reduction and a DEC wetland permit). A neighbor's engineer (Chris Morezello, for 1615 Old Orchard) raised three concerns: whether stormwater design accounted for climate change per the 2024 DEC manual, that the house remains among the largest by building coverage in the neighborhood, and driveway sight-distance/blind-spot safety. Jane Black reiterated the Conservation Board's view that the house should be smaller and in keeping with neighbors. The board defended the plan: the driveway conforms (200-foot sight line one way plus a variance), new construction is reasonably larger, footprint/impervious coverage sit within the neighborhood range, and the ten Cultec infiltrators exceed neighboring older homes' stormwater handling. The board declined to hold the applicant to a stricter-than-code future climate standard, closed the hearing, and approved the resolution as technically amended (septic reference corrected to sewer; DEC/NYC-DEP and plan-sheet conditions added).

cases.name: 111 Round Hill Road - rock crushing permit
cases.applicant: Robert Hoberman

timeline.summary: A lot-line realignment (no new lots, type-II SEQRA) combined with site plan and a special permit for an over-800-sq-ft accessory apartment; the applicant showed reduced clearing/grading, 108 proposed trees, and requested amending the 2002 clearing-and-grading limit line. The board agreed to a replanted buffer near property lines, voted to remove the required cistern (fire department won't maintain it) in favor of bedroom sprinklers, and set a public hearing for September 9.

The board held the public hearing and adopted preliminary and final subdivision/lot-line-change resolutions for 10 and 20 Round Hill Way, treating it as a SEQRA Type 2 action since no new lots are created, and amended the resolutions so the applicant's offered fire sprinklers apply only to second-floor bedrooms in lieu of the eliminated cisterns.
The board amended the extension resolution to reference the applicant's March 5, 2025 request for a 90-day extension and then approved the extension of time as amended.

Application to add rock crushing/processing to a previously approved site with rock chipping. The board debated noise, duration (about 30 crushing days, ~4,000 yards of rock), proximity to homes, and the fact that the more disruptive chipping/hammering is permitted separately by the building department without a hearing. It approved a crushing permit with a 10-week window at code hours; the motion carried with one dissent, and the board flagged wanting future coordination of chipping/hammering with crushing approvals.

cases.name: 22 Whippoorwill Road East
cases.address: 22 Whippoorwill Road East, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: owner/builder (Vladimir Levin, architect)
cases.lastStatus: public hearing closed; re-approved for 60 days with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing closed; re-approved for 60 days with conditions

timeline.summary: Review of a front-yard retaining wall and regrading that the owner had already begun building; the board was uneasy about the wall being constructed before approval but agreed it was likely the right solution and asked the applicant to return with site and landscape plans for a public hearing.

Public hearing on revisions to an as-built house that was constructed taller and with a foundation wall instead of porch piers; the board approved a mitigation plan using a tiered retaining wall with heavy plantings, adding two conditions (additional rear-yard evergreen screening and memorializing the neighbor-side/easement planting).

Request to extend a site plan approval whose conditions (an easement to the town attorney's satisfaction and a revised evergreen-screening landscaping plan) remain unfulfilled. A neighbor's attorney letter recited a history of stop-work orders and non-compliance and asked the board to hold the applicant's feet to the fire. Rather than the default one-year extension, the board granted a shorter extension to Feb 7, 2026, to require the applicant to submit the easement and landscaping paperwork; planting itself is enforced later by the building department at CO.

timeline.status: public hearing closed; re-approved for 60 days with conditions
timeline.summary: The applicant sought re-approval of a previously approved (and twice-expired) house project, now controlled by a bank after the developer defaulted. Members and the direct neighbor were frustrated that the front yard remains dirt, the railing is damaged, landscaping is unfinished, and the required easement for screening on the neighbor's property was never executed. The board debated how to protect the neighbor without making the house unsellable, ultimately granting only a 60-day approval (rather than a year) with conditions requiring execution of the easement, irrigation of the plantings on the neighbor's property for two years, and a maintenance bond for the planting plan. The hearing was closed and the amended resolution adopted.

cases.name: 130 Old Mount Kisco Road
cases.address: 130 Old Mount Kisco Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Frank Madonna (rep. Corey Salmer, Zarin & Steinman; engineer Ralph Alfonso)

timeline.summary: The board revisited this 3.2-acre two-lot conservation subdivision (last seen in 2021), discussed an unresolved code interpretation on whether one-acre frontage/lot-width standards apply, and moved to refer the applicant to the ZBA with a positive recommendation if the building inspector's ruling requires variances, while signaling intent to retain site plan jurisdiction.

Public hearing on a conservation subdivision of an oversized, steep mountainside lot with a conservation easement placed over the mountainside; a neighbor raised drought and well-water concerns, and the board directed the applicant to revise the conservation-easement line (to let a future buyer add a pool) and resubmit, keeping the hearing open.

Continued public hearing on a two-lot conservation subdivision revised to create a separate non-buildable conservation lot owned by both lots; the board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration plus preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.

Amendment to a previously approved three-lot conservation subdivision. While preparing the Mylar, a roughly 900-square-foot overlap with a neighboring property's deed was discovered; the applicant shifted the lot/reliance lines to comply, keeping Lots 1 and 2 the same size and reducing the conservation area by about 900 sq ft. Counsel advised no new hearing was needed since the plat was in substantial conformance with the preliminary. The board found conformance and adopted the amended final plat; a related time extension was also granted.

cases.name: 73 Whippoorwill Road Subdivision
cases.applicant: Wellness Estates LLC / Alice Gasky (engineer Louis de Marzo)

timeline.summary: Preliminary two-lot subdivision of an 8.8-acre parcel (Lot A 5.5 ac keeping the existing house, Lot B 3.3 ac conceptual new home); soils passed for septic and drainage. The board asked the applicant to either deed-restrict/conservation-easement Lot A or demonstrate a third lot isn't feasible given frontage/pond/steep slopes, and to detail any tree removal needed for the 200-ft sight line.

Public hearing on subdividing an 8.8-acre lot into a 5.5-acre Lot A and a 3.3-acre Lot B; the applicant's engineer addressed the 11 staff comments (school-bus pickup area, road-widening reservation, no-further-subdivision note, archaeological survey), the board kept site-plan jurisdiction over future development, and it asked the applicant to tighten the 21-condition resolution for later administrative approval.

Conditions-review for a subdivision where the hearing had been closed but too many conditions remained. Working with the engineering department, the applicant reduced the preliminary plat conditions from 15 to 3 and the final subdivision conditions from 21 to 10, all remaining items being tasks to complete rather than plan changes. The board adopted the NEG DEC and both the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.
Request for an extension of time on the subdivision, with the applicant dealing primarily with the Board of Health. The board granted the extension of time.

cases.name: 700 Bedford Road (new house)
cases.applicant: Joseph Casiotas (owner), represented by Elvis of Delhi Engineering

timeline.summary: First appearance before the Planning Board for a vertical and horizontal expansion (about 5,000 sq ft) of an existing single-family house plus a carriage house; the board reviewed site-plan, drainage/curb-cut and landscaping comments and referred the applicant to the ZBA (setback variance for the carriage house) and the ARB before returning.

Discussion of a site plan where the existing house has now been demolished and will be rebuilt on the existing foundation with a drive-through garage addition and improved gravel driveway. The board and engineer directed updated plans reflecting the fully new house, an expanded stormwater system designed for the 100-year storm, a more robust landscape/lighting plan, and confirmation of septic and DOT curb-cut items before scheduling the required public hearing.

The applicant seeks approval for a new house, with open issues on whether the county health department will accept the existing septic, NYSDOT right-of-way/curb-cut requirements, and whether the board will allow two curb cuts where code prefers one. The board was skeptical of retaining two curb cuts and pressed the applicant to document line-of-sight from each and consider a single reconfigured curb cut. Members debated a conditional approval tied to a health-department 'no objection' letter for the septic. The board scheduled a site walk for the following week and clarified that a noticed public hearing still must be conducted before any approval.

The board reviewed a recent site walk though no one appeared for the applicant. The property was described as effectively a blank slate showing existing conditions, and the board recommended the applicant hire a landscape architect to dial in the plan. The applicant is developing plans behind the scenes per prior feedback and is expected to return.

cases.name: Whippoorwill Club amended site plan and tree removal, 148 Whippoorwill Road
cases.applicant: Whippoorwill Club, represented by Jim Ryan (formerly JMC) and superintendent Paul Gonzalez

timeline.summary: The club sought approval to remove 54 trees (37 near holes 15 and 16) as part of a course restoration, plus removal of two trees within a man-made pond's wetland buffer. The board asked to see the site before deciding, scheduled a Wednesday site visit and set a public hearing for the March 24 meeting; the two buffer trees could be handled administratively if deemed minor wetlands.

The club presented revised plans to remove trees and add a raised 16th tee box, sand trap and screening plantings, but the board directed it to submit a comprehensive amended site plan (with elevations and fill quantities) before approval and adjourned the hearing held open.

Continued public hearing on an amended site plan and tree-removal permit for golf course changes at the 15th and 16th holes (tee boxes, a restored sand trap, grading and removal of roughly 54 trees); neighbors and the Conservation Board pushed back hard on tree loss and mitigation, and the hearing was kept open for further engineering review and another site walk.

Amended site plan and tree-removal permit for relocating the 16th tee box (~24 ft north, ~18 ft east) with adjusted grading and added screening plantings; 34 new plantings against 39 trees removed, most work outside the NYC DEP conservation easement (DEP permits removal of healthy trees within the easement). Added plan notes commit the club to coordinate final plantings with the neighbor/town and to remedy any future stormwater/drainage impacts on abutting properties, with disputes returning to the planning board. The public hearing was reopened and closed and the application approved.

cases.name: 7 Hollow Ridge Road (Wood Hollow Estates)
cases.address: 7 Hollow Ridge Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: owner/builder John Nickett; represented by Ralph Alpinsetti

trajectory.status: discussion only (public hearing to be scheduled; referral to ARB/RPRC)

timeline.status: discussion only (public hearing to be scheduled; referral to ARB/RPRC)
timeline.summary: A working discussion on developing a vacant 2.5-acre subdivision lot (no wetlands, sewer in the road) with a ~7,500-8,000 sq ft house comparable to neighbors, involving substantial cut and fill between a high and low grade. The planner suggested retaining walls to reduce cut, and the board explored slope steepness, a rock outcrop, and whether the design could include a walk-out basement under the current 30/38-foot height rules. The builder cited a nearly identical prior house he built on Terrace Circle; the board directed responses to the engineer's and planner's memos, a possible pre-submission meeting, and then a public hearing.

Continuation of a hearing on a single-family house with pool, patio, driveway and stormwater capture. The applicant reported reducing the disturbance area (from ~71,700 to ~62,000 sf) and tree removal (from 134 to 99). Much of the discussion centered on the town engineer's (John Kellard) memo, which had arrived late and which the applicant team had not yet seen: knoll grading, ~10-foot driveway cuts on a 14% grade, rock outcroppings, the need for a temporary sediment trap rather than just silt fence, and trench drains for driveway runoff. The board declined to adopt the resolution until the applicant reviews and addresses the memo, keeping the hearing open and adjourning. Landscaping (six white pines for rear screening) was also debated.

The resumed hearing covered erosion control, grading and drainage worked out that afternoon with town engineer John Kellard, including trench-drain sump structures, two temporary sediment basins, construction ditch relocation to the toe of slope, and possibly removing a rear retaining wall so drainage could be consolidated to the front. Roughly 22 trees may be removed and the drip-line grading impacts remain undefined. A neighbor's letter about screening was addressed via a resolution condition adding 20 green-giant arborvitae. The chair concluded the plans were too incomplete to approve and sent the applicant back to finalize drawings with the engineer before returning.

Continued public hearing on a residential site plan. The landscaping plan had been enhanced, with 21 green giant arborvitae shown in the rear versus the 20 requested, and a well permit from the Health Department was in hand. The town engineer noted that drip lines showed the tree-removal count increasing from 99 to 131 and required the site to be stabilized before framing, with those revisions on the plan. Board members had no further questions; the board closed the public hearing and adopted the site plan resolution.

cases.name: 65 Bedford-Banksville Road (Buck's Flower Garden)
cases.applicant: P. Daniel Hollis (attorney) and Joseph Rina (engineer) for the property owner

trajectory.status: discussion only; April 8 site walk scheduled

timeline.summary: Applicant sought amendment of a 1980 special permit for a nursery operation, adding a small retail farm stand, a rebuilt family residence, two horses/barn, expanded garage with offices, and planting areas, with the matter to be referred back to the town board as lead agency. The board discussed conflicts with the old permit (planting near wetlands/wells, building heights, retail prohibition) and traffic-safety concerns at the entrance, and agreed to schedule a joint work session with the conservation board rather than act tonight.

timeline.status: discussion only; April 8 site walk scheduled
timeline.summary: A ~46-year family wholesale nursery with a single-family home that accrued building-department violations, chiefly an unpermitted fill/boulder retaining area (~700+ cubic yards) with no fill certification, plus an unpermitted loop road, expired sign permit and other cleanup items. The applicant seeks to legalize the site while reducing nursery intensity (abandoning retail) and building a new home and barn/garage. Staff's memo argued the town board must re-approve the special use permit due to increased intensity of use (office and equipment garage space); the board wants a narrative of operations. Concerns focused on possible contamination in the undocumented fill (soil/core sampling via HES to be initiated) and tree removal for a proposed third horse paddock. The board scheduled a site walk for April 8 at 8:30 AM, partly so new member Thomas Crispi could see the property, and left the item open for further discussion in April.

This was a continuation discussing the board's recent site walk of the former nursery site. The key open items were verifying imported fill/soils (an HES sampling protocol is being prepared and HES will visit the site), unpermitted retaining walls the owner created, and a possibly relocated gravel road. Town counsel (Mary) clarified the board cannot itself decide whether an amended special-use permit is needed - that determination rests with the building inspector (Rob) - while the applicant argued they are reducing the level of activity. The applicant is under court-deadline pressure (adjourned to May 29) to move quickly. A curb-cut discrepancy in the memos was clarified as an existing display area, not a new curb cut.

cases.name: 32 Orchard Drive subdivision (re-approval)
cases.applicant: Whitney Singleton (Singleton, Davis & Singleton), on behalf of applicant

timeline.summary: Public hearing on a five-lot (four new) subdivision of a ~13-acre R-1A parcel; extensive neighbor concern about steep slopes, stormwater, septic and well/aquifer impacts led the board to keep the hearing open, engage the town's hydrogeologist, and keep the lots under Planning Board (not RPRC) jurisdiction so each future house gets a public hearing.

The board reopened and closed the public hearing and adopted a negative declaration plus preliminary and final subdivision plat approvals with steep-slope and tree-removal permits, after an extended discussion of well/groundwater adequacy on the bedrock aquifer and of tightening the clearing-and-grading limit line to protect a steep slope.

Because the prior approval had expired, the five-lot subdivision of the 12.9-acre R1A parcel returned unchanged; the board opened and closed the hearing and adopted the negative declaration plus preliminary and final subdivision approvals.

cases.name: 23 Bedford-Banksville Road (special use permit and site-plan extension)
cases.applicant: Property owner (Anthony, attorney; Peter Gregory, plans)

timeline.summary: Continued public hearing to legalize a rehabbed formerly-vacant building whose uses straddle two zoning districts; the board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the site plan and wetlands permit as amended, resolving how contaminated fill removal would be tested/monitored (DEC and/or town).

The board reviewed a petition, referred by the town board, to rezone the split-zoned parcel entirely into CBB and add a special-use permit allowing existing wood-processing and pre-cut metal/aluminum assemblage uses; the board voted to recommend adoption with added limits (use confined to roughly the rear 50% of the building not fronting the road, ground floor only, with a separate entrance).

Now that the whole parcel is in the CBB district and code was amended to permit the rear special-permit uses, the board made a positive recommendation to the town board on the special use permit and, after amending its agenda, granted a one-year extension of time on the previously approved site plan.

cases.name: 60 Cox Avenue (Breezemont Day Camp)
cases.applicant: Breezemont day camp (Walter, with engineer Dan Holt)

timeline.summary: Referred back from the Town Board, the board discussed legalizing the existing day camp via site plan, focusing on the required 15-foot landscaped screening buffer adjacent to residences and summer vehicle parking/traffic; no approval tonight, and a site walk was scheduled (the 18th) before setting a public hearing.

Public hearing held on a site plan memorializing the existing day camp (now a permitted special-use); the only new construction is a front parking lot with a pervious paver section for drainage. After discussion of a discretionary conservation-board referral for parcels over 10 acres (deemed inapplicable since this is not a new subdivision/development), the hearing was closed and the resolution approved.

The board discussed a proposed site plan amendment to formalize on-site overflow parking for special events and staff training days at the Breezemont camp, prompted by the building department. The applicant emphasized nothing changes for the regular camp season, when hundreds of attendees are still shuttled in by bus, and the extra spaces would be used only a few days a year. Members raised concerns about spaces directly on Cox Avenue being visible and unscreened, and asked that the newly added spaces be clearly marked in color on a revised map so they can be distinguished from previously approved spaces. The matter will proceed to a noticed public hearing.

cases.name: Kent Place / Verizon Parking (23 Whippoorwill Road East)
cases.address: 23 Whippoorwill Road East, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Verizon

trajectory.status: approved (negative declaration, site plan, preliminary and final subdivision resolutions adopted)

timeline.summary: The board adopted the draft resolution granting an extension of time for the Ken Place Verizon parking plan as procedural closing business.

timeline.status: approved (negative declaration, site plan, preliminary and final subdivision resolutions adopted)
timeline.summary: A re-approval of an already-built parking expansion whose original approvals expired because Verizon never signed the plat map; no changes to what was built. A long-time abutting neighbor (Suzanne) testified at length about Verizon's chronic lack of maintenance, tree removal without replacement, an unstabilized dirt frontage with U-turns and a porta-potty, a downed fence, and unfinished screening she paid ~$40,000 to remedy herself. The board acknowledged those are largely building-department property-maintenance matters, advised her to write the building department, and re-adopted all resolutions so the plat can be filed with the health department.

The board granted an extension of time for the Ken Place Verizon parking plan. Staff reported the required Verizon signatures had finally been obtained and the matter now rests with the department of health, and that the applicant's variance had been renewed about a year ago so there is no variance concern.

cases.name: 18 Long Pond Road
cases.address: 18 Long Pond Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Daniel and Joanna Novick (landscape architect Dean Portula)

timeline.summary: Introduction of a swimming pool proposal entirely within a 100-foot wetland buffer on a constrained, sloping lot; the board referred it to the Conservation Board and scheduled a joint site visit, with stormwater and mitigation plans still being engineered.

Referral back from the Conservation Board (which was split, with only four of seven members present) on a pool, spa, and patio within a wetland buffer. The applicant reduced the pool and patio (~25-50%), increased the wetland setback from about 12 to 19-20 feet, and raised mitigation planting to three-to-one to convert a low-functioning wetland to higher-functioning. Conservation liaison Jane Black explained the split: two members found the property would be improved by the mitigation, while dissenters objected over a culvert/former stream location and the small backyard size. The Board was favorable, viewing it as a net positive for the wetland and a reasonable suburban amenity, and directed that a public hearing be scheduled (in November).

The board opened and closed a public hearing on a swimming pool, patio, deck modification, tree removal and landscaping within a regulated wetland buffer, ultimately approving the site plan, wetlands permit and tree removal permit. The landscape architect described a stormwater plan storing pool drawdown with slow release, an extensive planting plan providing 3x mitigation, elimination of pesticides, and habitat features; diseased beech trees would be removed. The Conservation Board deadlocked 2-2, with the town engineer explaining both sides: some members opposed 'rewarding' new disturbance on a site with a decades-old buried water course, while others saw the mitigation as a net improvement to a low-functioning wetland. The board examined topography, whether the existing 60+ year-old pipe still functions, and read a neighbor's email opposing the project despite the mitigation explanation.

cases.name: 825 North Broadway (BP gas station renovation)
cases.applicant: Gas station owner (represented by a consulting engineer)

timeline.summary: The board reviewed the revised gas-station plan covering pump circulation, removal of car-washing stations, stormwater infiltration, canopy size, landscaping and streetscape/sidewalk upgrades, and directed the applicant to the Architectural Review Board before returning for a hearing.

Public hearing on a site-plan application to renovate the interior, replace fuel pumps and underground storage tanks, rebuild the convenience store with a gable roof, and improve circulation, lighting, retaining walls and stormwater. No members of the public appeared. The board focused on a pump-queuing/circulation problem (cars stacking at the three in-line pumps blocking one another) and whether a 'pull forward' sign or full-service operation could mitigate it; the applicant agreed to raise full service with the owner. Rather than adopt the draft resolution, the board closed the hearing and sent the applicant home to satisfy the many open conditions (stormwater calcs for the 25-year event, upsized pipes to 8-inch minimum, ARB stone-pillar condition) and return with a tightened, near-final resolution before the building department stage.

Status update only on the 825 North Broadway gas station. Staff reported the board had previously been comfortable with the plan and requested a draft resolution, but outstanding comments remained, so the applicant made a further submission that addressed many but not all conditions. The town engineer still could not recommend adoption, so the applicant will make another submission. No action was taken.

cases.name: 167 Mianus River Road (Mianus River Gorge)
cases.address: 167 Mianus River Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Mianus River Gorge Inc.

trajectory.status: public hearing opened and adjourned without date

timeline.status: public hearing opened and adjourned without date
timeline.summary: Public hearing to construct an office addition and a gravel parking lot on the 960-acre preserve property in the R4A zone. Steven Sauro read the public hearing notice. The town planner advised that the applicant must first obtain an amended special use permit from the Town Board before the Planning Board can proceed. With no neighbors present, the board opened and immediately adjourned the hearing without a date.

The applicant sought site plan approval for a science-education office addition and a gravel parking lot (reduced from 10 to 8 spaces), with variances already granted by the ZBA and stormwater handled via infiltration trenches on a low-sensitivity, non-watershed site. A revised plan had been submitted only the prior week, after the deadline, and the applicant had not yet obtained Architectural Review Board approval, which the resolution would have made a post-approval condition. The chair objected on process grounds, preferring the applicant obtain ARB approval first and return with a clean submission rather than set a precedent. The board carried the matter over, placing the applicant on the September 25 agenda after the ARB's September 17 meeting; the applicant can begin assembling building-permit materials in the meantime.

Continuation of a public hearing on an addition to the non-profit nature center, including a building expansion for office space, a new septic system, an overflow parking area, and stormwater management. The only change from the prior meeting was a reduction of two parking spaces, revising the layout from stacked to directly accessed spaces, and leaving the existing paved driveway as-is. No members of the public spoke; the board closed the hearing and approved the site plan. The board praised the applicant's engineering work.

cases.name: 258 East Middle Patent Road (Matthews accessory barn)
cases.address: 258 East Middle Patent Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Chris Salabarria & Carol Matthews (engineer Allen Pilch, ALP Engineering)

trajectory.status: referred (to ZBA; also ARB and Conservation Board)

timeline.status: referred (to ZBA; also ARB and Conservation Board)
timeline.summary: Initial concept presentation to replace a 100-plus-year-old dilapidated barn/garage with a combined garage and accessory apartment, intended primarily to give the owners' wheelchair-using adult son accessible visits since the existing home has interior steps. The structure is beyond saving (crumbling foundation), so the project needs several variances and touches the wetland buffer with a small portion of an ADA ramp and stormwater mitigation, requiring Conservation Board review. The chair suggested the applicants consider whether the existing footprint is truly the best location. The board referred the applicant to the ZBA and agreed to refer to the Conservation Board.

Discussion of an accessory dwelling unit in a barn/garage building, before the board for a wetland permit, scenic-road frontage and a special permit. The applicant reported that after an October site walk and a follow-up meeting the Conservation Board was satisfied with the wetland permit and mitigation, with buffer impacts reduced from over 2,400 sq ft to 1,514 sq ft (about 70 sq ft for a handicap ramp plus stormwater and a relocated rain garden). Invasive species (Oriental bittersweet, mugwort, multiflora rose) would be removed and a mitigation planting plan provided; percolation testing was to be witnessed by the town engineer. The board found the application strong and scheduled the public hearing (targeted for the December meeting, ultimately the 24th) with a draft resolution to follow.

The board opened and closed a public hearing and approved the site plan for a detached accessory apartment (over 800 sq ft) in a renovated garage/barn to accommodate an owner's mobility needs, including a wheelchair-accessible ramp, new septic for the barn, and stormwater/rain garden improvements. The engineer reported no direct wetland impacts, minor wetland-buffer impacts offset by invasive removal and native plantings, and successful percolation testing. Members debated resolution conditions at length: whether the building-permit trigger tied to Department of Health approval should be relaxed given DOH delays, the redundant existing-septic review condition, and a weekly stormwater-inspection reporting requirement (condition 10) the applicant felt was onerous. The board kept the DOH condition intact but clarified the septic language applies to the barn, and approved the site plan.

cases.name: 250 East Middle Patent Road
cases.address: 250 East Middle Patent Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Neil and Vanessa Lucy (owners); attorney Michael Sirignano; Jerry Barrett (landscape architect) and Nicholas of Hudson Engineering

timeline.summary: A pool application first seen ~5 years ago under prior owners (the Benises) returned with the Lucy family. After a site conversation with the chair, the team presented a sketch moving the pool 16 feet back and about 4 feet lower so it sits in the side yard rather than the front yard, eliminating the zoning setback variance but still implicating the scenic road overlay, a conservation buffer, and 25% slopes. The revised concept would tie the pool to the existing bluestone patio via a retaining/engineered wall (est. 6-8 ft) with a forward sitting wall. The board strongly endorsed the new direction and asked the applicant to formalize plans with landscape and wetland mitigation plans and return.

Following a site walk the prior week, the board reviewed a revised plan that pulls the structure a full 16 feet further from the road and roughly 18 feet lower in elevation, making it essentially not visible. Members found it favorably sited and no longer in the front yard. A wetland permit is triggered because the work is within 150 feet of the wetland, and discussion clarified the steep-slope (25%) regulation, with engineer John Kellard noting the rear yard is under 25% which narrows the review. The board voted to refer the applicant to the Conservation Board, targeting a September public hearing on return.

The applicant sought to install a swimming pool on a property fronting scenic East Middle Patent Road. After a prior version needed a variance, the board's site-walk feedback led the applicant to move the pool back 16 feet and 4 feet lower in elevation, eliminating the front-yard setback variance (edge of water ~79 feet versus 75-foot setback). Sections were cut to show minimal visibility from the road, aided by existing vegetation, rock forms, and proposed landscaping, with an engineered rear wall not visible from the road. The board praised the collaborative result, closed the hearing, and approved the site plan.

cases.name: Summit Golf Club
cases.address: Summit Golf Club, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners

trajectory.status: extensions of time granted (site plan and 8th/final subdivision 90-day)

timeline.summary: The board considered two extensions of time for the Summit Club: one for the final subdivision plat approval and one for the site plan (with steep slopes and tree-removal permit approvals). Staff explained the applicant is working through the approval process and is reportedly taking deposits/listing units for sale, with the county Board of Health notoriously slow on the substantial infrastructure (including a sewage treatment plant). The board granted both extensions of time.

timeline.status: extensions of time granted (site plan and 8th/final subdivision 90-day)
timeline.summary: The project is awaiting Westchester County Health Department approval for a pump station, tank and water/sewer system, expected to be approved together. The board granted an extension of time on the site plan approval and the eighth (final) 90-day extension on the final subdivision plat.

No representative was present. The chair and planner gave an update noting background activity on water infrastructure: a water-line extension easement is already in place, but the timeline may accelerate so that water could be brought through the club and interconnected (potentially reaching Windmill), rather than the development operating as its own on-site water district. The board granted an extension of time.

cases.name: 2 Israel Townsend Hill (Lot 1, 32 Orchard Drive subdivision)
cases.address: 2 Israel Townsend Hill, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: 32 Orto Drive LLC; Andrew Vaccarello, B&J Engineering; colleague Matt (architect)

trajectory.status: public hearing opened | public hearing continued

timeline.summary: Site plan for a single-family dwelling on Lot 1 of a recorded subdivision over which the board retained jurisdiction. The ~2,900 sq ft footprint is fully zoning compliant with generous setbacks; it is about 700 sq ft larger than previously depicted with a slightly enlarged driveway in the same location, an on-site septic and well, a rain garden for the slight impervious overage, reduced downstream peak flows, and about 24 trees removed. Members discussed the landscaping/replanting plan and tree preservation, and the board directed the applicant to the ARB, asking that a landscape plan be brought along.

timeline.status: public hearing opened | public hearing continued
timeline.summary: New four-bedroom single-family dwelling with three-car garage on a subdivision lot, replacing an existing tennis court, with septic, well, driveway and stormwater (shared BMP plus a rain garden); 24 trees to be removed. Neighbors Darren and Susan Lampert (24 Orchard Drive, 25-year residents directly behind the lot) objected that shrubbery is inadequate and asked for tall staggered evergreen screening along the driveway and rear, citing loss of privacy, headlight glare, and the home's height. The applicant agreed to add staggered evergreens of mixed species and proposed eliminating the rear rain garden to save trees and redirect flow to the shared BMP. The board kept the public hearing open pending a revised landscape plan, targeting the next meeting (Oct 16) alongside another subdivision lot.

Continued public hearing on new house construction with a tree-removal permit. In response to prior direction for a 'robust planting plan,' the applicant added 12 trees (8 Arborvitae, 4 Eastern Hemlock) integrated with existing vegetation along the neighbor's property line for headlight/visual screening, and removed a rain garden to save trees. The neighbor (Darren Lampert) objected that the proposed 4-foot trees were insufficient. The Board closed the hearing and approved the site development plan and tree-removal permit, conditioned on noting the prior-day ARB approval and revising the planting schedule to 8-10 foot trees.

cases.name: 4 Vincent Lane (wetland restoration)
cases.applicant: Lewis Fusco, landscape architect, for owners Tom and Sarah DeSwart

trajectory.status: public hearing closed; decision adjourned pending ARB approval of existing sheds/barn

timeline.summary: New owners seek to modify the existing driveway (new circular drive) and re-wild the property with native plantings while memorializing prior work done without Planning Board approval (a pool built under a building permit, several sheds, and turf/paved areas in wetland buffers). The plan reduces land coverage from over 23,000 sq ft to under the approved 19,000 and removes turf/paving from wetland buffers; wetlands were flagged by a specialist and invasives are being removed. The board viewed the request as largely procedural memorialization and directed coordination with the Conservation Board, which will do a site visit before sending a memo back to the Planning Board.

timeline.status: public hearing closed; decision adjourned pending ARB approval of existing sheds/barn
timeline.summary: A wetlands/site-plan application to modify a driveway and front walkway, remove astroturf golf areas and invasive wetland plants, and install native plantings, removing roughly 25,000 sq ft of lawn/hardscape and providing 40,000 sq ft of wetland mitigation. The Conservation Board had commended the project and the applicant addressed the town engineer's comments.
